text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNConnect spherical collapse, Gaussian tails, and mass-to-number conversion, explaining the factor of two and model limits. Connect to foundations: Cosmic expansion and the Hubble–Lemaître law ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01From small fluctuations to halo abundances Regions slightly denser than the cosmic mean can attract more matter. Press–Schechter theory combines fluctuation statistics with a collapse criterion to estimate halo abundances by mass. A halo here means a gravitationally bound dark-matter structure. Define density contrast δ, initially with |δ| ≪ 1. Include cosmic expansion and pressureless matter growth, extending beyond the static gas in the Jeans chapter. The statistical variable is the linearly extrapolated contrast; the actual late nonlinear density field is not assumed to remain Gaussian. δ ≡ ρ−ρ̄ρ̄, δL(t) = D(t)δL(t₀), D(t₀) = 1 Playback uses a flat, matter-only Einstein–de Sitter universe: D = a, a(t₀) = 1, and a ∝ t2/3. This is not an assertion that D = a remains exact at low redshift in ΛCDM. 02Choose a mass scale by smoothing Averages over small and large regions need not agree. Smooth the field with a normalized window W and call its rms fluctuation σ(M,t). A real-space top-hat averages uniformly within a comoving radius R, which differs from the final halo radius. M = 4π3ρ̄m,0R³, σ²(M,t) ≡ ⟨δL,R²⟩ σ(M,t) = D(t)σ(M,t₀) Here ρ̄m,0 is the mean matter density at the reference epoch, matching the comoving volume used for number densities. Linear smoothing of an initially Gaussian field gives a zero-mean Gaussian with variance σ². p(δL|M,t) = 1√(2π)σexp(−δL²2σ²) σ measures fluctuation strength at a mass scale, not the density of an individual halo. A larger σ places more of the distribution above a fixed threshold. 03Spherical collapse gives a threshold of 1.686 Model a uniform overdense region as a pressureless sphere. Before shell crossing, each shell encloses constant mass M and obeys R̈ = −GM/R². The growing-mode solution can be written parametrically: R = A(1−cos θ), t = B(θ−sin θ), A³ = GMB² The sphere turns around at θ = π and formally reaches R = 0 at θ = 2π. Divide its density 3M/(4πR³) by the background density 1/(6πGt²) to obtain the nonlinear contrast. 1+δNL = 92(θ−sin θ)²(1−cos θ)³ At small θ, θ−sinθ ≈ θ³/6 and δNL ≈ 3θ²/20. Match this to linear growth proportional to t2/3, then extrapolate: δL(θ) = 35[34(θ−sin θ)]2/3 δc = δL(2π) = 35(3π2)2/3 ≈ 1.68647 1.686 is a linearly extrapolated contrast at the formal collapse time, not the actual halo overdensity. Real halos undergo shell crossing and virialization; the singular R = 0 solution does not describe their internal evolution. 04Relate a Gaussian tail to a mass fraction Define peak height ν = δc/σ. A smaller σ makes the same threshold rarer. First compute the probability P of exceeding it at one smoothing scale by substituting u = δL/σ. P = ∫ν∞e−u²/2√(2π)du = 12erfc(ν√2) The Press–Schechter prescription assigns mass fraction F(>M) = 2P to halos above M. The complementary error function erfc is a name for this Gaussian-tail integral, not an additional physical law. F(>M,t) = erfc(ν√2), ν = δcσ(M,t) For ν = 1, P ≈ 0.1587 and F ≈ 0.3173; at ν = 2, F ≈ 0.04550, and at ν = 3, F ≈ 0.002700. The Gaussian tail makes high-ν objects rare. The factor of two has not yet been derived; it requires the next section. 05The factor of two and cloud-in-cloud accounting A region below threshold on one scale can lie inside a larger collapsing region. Smaller regions inside a larger halo can also be counted as separate objects. A single-scale tail probability alone does not consistently assign matter to halos. Even as σ → ∞, P approaches only 1/2. Doubling restores total-mass normalization, but symmetry between positive and negative contrasts alone does not solve the nested-region problem. Excursion-set theory follows one position from large smoothing scales to small ones and assigns mass at the first threshold crossing. A Gaussian field with a sharp-k window and constant barrier has independent random-walk increments; a reflection argument yields the factor of two. Extension: the first-crossing distribution S ≡ σ², ffirst(S) = δc√(2π)S3/2exp(−δc²2S) F(>M) = ∫0S(M)ffirst(S)dS We supply the reflection-principle result without solving a diffusion equation here. Real-space top-hat and Gaussian windows correlate the steps, so this simple derivation cannot be transferred unchanged. Distinguish the PS prescription, including its mass–window mapping, from the conditions of an exact first-crossing solution. 06Convert mass fractions into number densities Let n(M,t)dM be the number of halos per comoving volume in the interval [M,M+dM]. Minus the differential of F gives the mass fraction in this interval. Multiply by mean comoving matter density and divide by the mass per halo. M n(M,t)dM = −ρ̄m,0∂F∂MdM When ν increases with M, ∂F/∂ν = −√(2/π)exp(−ν²/2) and ∂ν/∂M = (ν/M)|∂lnσ/∂lnM|. Apply the chain rule: n(M,t) = √(2π)ρ̄m,0M²ν|∂lnσ∂lnM|e−ν²/2 n has units of inverse comoving volume per unit mass. Number per natural-log mass is Mn(M), whereas mass fraction per natural-log mass is ψ = M²n(M)/ρ̄m,0. These are distinct vertical axes and give different curve shapes. ψ(M,t) ≡ M²n(M,t)ρ̄m,0, ∫0∞ψ(M,t)dlnM = 1 This is the distribution of halos present at each epoch, not a formation rate per unit time. Merger histories require further ingredients such as conditional mass distributions. Total-mass normalization assumes monotonically increasing σ reaching infinity as M → 0. Do not impose it unchanged on a model with a small-scale cutoff. 07Use a power-law spectrum to expose time scaling The power spectrum describes fluctuation strength by wavenumber. For P(k) ∝ kn and a window W(kR), substitute q = kR to factor out the radius dependence. Spectral index n is distinct from the mass-function notation n(M). σ²(R) = 12π²∫0∞k²P(k)|W(kR)|²dk ∝ R−(n+3) σ(M,t) ∝ D(t)M−p, p = n+36 For a real-space top-hat, a pure power law extending over all wavenumbers converges for −3 < n < 1. The panel stays within this idealized range; it does not compute a transfer function or calibrate σ₈ for precision cosmology. σ(M,t) = δcD(t)(MM₀)−p, ν = (M/M₀)pD(t) σ(M*,t) = δc ⇒ M*M₀ = D1/p M₀ is an arbitrary reference mass where ν = 1 at D = 1. M* also maximizes the mass-weighted logarithmic distribution ψ. For n = −2, p = 1/6 and M* ∝ D⁶. Scaling the horizontal axis by M* makes curves at fixed n overlap. 08What the plots do and do not reproduce These teaching plots recompute the equations above. To compare with Bond et al. (1991), equation (3.9), identify their A with S = σ², their fᵥ with δc, and |dlnA/dlnM| with 2p. This gives the same ψ = √(2/π)pνexp(−ν²/2). Equivalently, keep A = σ²(t₀) fixed and use barrier fᵥ = δc/D(t) to obtain the same ν. Checks cover the analytic expression, standard Gaussian-tail values, mass normalization, and time scaling. These are not copies of paper figures, N-body data, or curves using a CDM transfer function. For example, Bond et al. Figure 5a uses a CDM spectrum, unlike this power-law model. Distinguish recomputing an equation, reproducing a named figure, and comparing measured data. A citation alone does not make curves computed under different conditions identical. 09From dark halos to luminous galaxies PS theory bridges initial fluctuations and halo statistics. It does not specify gas cooling, star-formation efficiency, supernova or active-galactic-nucleus heating, or post-merger morphology. One halo cannot automatically be equated with one observed luminous galaxy. Predictions depend on spherical-collapse assumptions, filtering, and nonspherical dynamics. Use this chapter to understand exponential rarity and hierarchical formation, with simulation-calibrated mass functions needed for more precise observational predictions. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. For P(k) ∝ k⁻², halve D from 1. How does M* change? At fixed M = M₀, what happens to ν and F(>M)? Show the answer and reasoning p = 1/6, so M* ∝ D⁶ and decreases by 64. At fixed M₀, ν rises from 1 to 2 and F falls from about 0.3173 to 0.04550. This is a fraction of mass in halos heavier than M₀, not a fraction of halo counts. REFERENCES & PHYSICAL INPUTS Explanations and derivations are written for this guide.
